Innings: 2
Fields:
- inn2.total_runs

Commentary:
Good morning from Brookmere Cricket Ground in North Valley, with Daniel Foster and Peter Lane already set in the middle and Emily Carter watching the formal pieces from the side, and Ridgefield CC’s choice to bat first began to feel uncomfortable almost as soon as the new ball started asking its questions, because this was not one of those bright mornings where the first ten overs simply glide by and the openers build without consequence. Ethan Marsh kept the first end tight enough to make every forward press feel like a decision, Jacob Stone found the fuller length that kept bringing bat and pad into the conversation, and Ridgefield’s opening movement came as much from Valleygate’s occasional looseness as from anything truly imposed by the batters. Noah Pierce was the first to go, pinned in front before he had ever looked settled, and Adrian Wells, after one decent stroke and a little survival work, followed soon after when Stone drew the catch that made the top order look fragile rather than merely cautious. From there the innings quickly narrowed. Caleb Ross came and went without scoring, Ryan Cole only briefly interrupted the pressure, and at 19 for 4 the whole batting plan had already collapsed into the much smaller job of staying alive. Lucas Bennett became the one constant, not fluent, not dominant, but stubborn enough to make the innings last longer than it felt capable of lasting, and when Mason Doyle joined him there was at least a short passage where Ridgefield looked like they might drag the match into something resembling a contest. Doyle’s 10 was modest, but in context it mattered because he gave Bennett the only partnership that had any real body to it, the pair taking the score past the worst of the early wreckage and forcing Valleygate to work through a slightly longer spell rather than simply collect wickets in clusters. That was exactly where Mason Hale changed the innings from damaged to nearly broken. He removed Doyle when that stand was beginning to look like a small repair, then went through Owen Scott soon after, and the feel of the match shifted again because Ridgefield had not merely lost another batter, they had lost the one stretch in which the score had been moving with any shape. Tyler Quinn gave Bennett the next bit of company and pushed the total into the sixties, but Samuel Cross bowled him before that stand could grow into a true recovery, and once Finn Carter was also removed the tail was almost out of road. Hale returned to take Liam Brooks and then Jack Reed, leaving Bennett stranded on 21 not out and Ridgefield all out for 74 in 24.5 overs. The total was not disastrous only because Bennett refused to disappear and because the extras column kept contributing in small, untidy ways, but the batting itself had produced very little control: one not-out hand, one brief captain’s stand, Tyler’s small resistance, and too many entries that ended before the innings could rebuild around them. Valleygate’s attack was balanced in the way low-score bowling performances need to be. Marsh started the squeeze, Stone did the major early damage with three wickets, Cross made sure the lower order could not stretch the total into a more awkward range, and Hale’s 4 for 17 gave the innings its decisive shape. Chasing 75, Valleygate still needed to avoid the one thing small targets can create, which is self-inflicted panic, and Oliver Grant plus Aaron Blake began with enough calm to make Ridgefield work for their first lift. Grant did fall to Mason Doyle, but the opening stand had already taken the target out of the most dangerous new-ball pocket. Aaron Blake then played the firmer early hand, and with Kevin Hall he moved Valleygate to 50 before Tyler Quinn removed him. There was a tiny flicker when Ethan Marsh was trapped shortly after, the score only just past the halfway line in emotional terms even if the target was small, but Hall never let Ridgefield turn that flicker into a final act. He stayed clear, picked the right balls to hit, and once Brian Lewis arrived the finish became sudden. Lewis’ unbeaten 19 from five balls changed the chase from controlled to emphatic, a couple of clean boundary blows turning what might have been a careful ten-over job into a quick close. Hall stayed not out on 28, Lewis finished beside him, and Valleygate reached 76 for 3 in 10.2 overs. Ridgefield had their moments with the ball through Doyle and Quinn, but defending 74 requires near-perfection, and they did not have enough runs or enough wickets in hand on the scoreboard to make Valleygate truly doubt the chase. The match therefore resolves cleanly: Ridgefield chose to bat, were broken open by Stone and then finished by Hale, Lucas Bennett alone holding the innings together from inside the collapse; Valleygate lost three wickets in reply, but Kevin Hall’s calm and Brian Lewis’ sharp finish made the chase feel properly under control. Mason Hale was the correct player of the match because his spell cut through the only Ridgefield passages that looked as though they might develop into recovery, and once that innings had been held to 74, the rest of the match was mostly about Valleygate completing a job their bowlers had already made small.

Commentary:
At Alderfield Oval in Northmere, under a sky that looked calm enough before the first ball and then slowly turned into one of those long afternoons where the fielding side begins by believing it has a plan and ends up chasing shadows, Brookhaven CC won the toss and chose to bat first, and for a short while Stonebridge CC had enough discipline to make that call look only cautiously correct rather than obviously dominant. Henry Cole and Marcus Flynn were not spraying early, and the first ten overs had a proper contest inside them, Noah Clarke taking the busier opening role while Adrian Vale started with the sort of quiet measurement that can look almost harmless until the field suddenly realizes the batter has read the pace better than everyone else. Clarke’s 28 gave Brookhaven the first platform, and when he was eventually taken off Henry Cole with the score in the mid-sixties, Stonebridge could still tell themselves they had not let the game run away. That feeling did not last, because the second act of the innings belonged almost entirely to Adrian Vale. Ethan Brooks was the partner who gave the stand its balance, not always fluent, not trying to dominate, but steady enough to keep the bowlers from locking every plan around one man, while Vale kept opening out, first through controlled driving, then through harder strokes square of the wicket, then through those lifted hits that tell a captain the normal ring field has already lost its authority. The partnership moved past a hundred and carried Brookhaven from a good start into command, and even though there were a few gifts tucked into the total, the main pressure was coming from the bat. Vale’s retirement hurt on 118 changed the visual rhythm of the innings, but not its direction. He had already built the architecture of the match, and Stonebridge were left with the awkward feeling that they had not dismissed the one batter who had done most of the damage. Ethan Brooks and Lucas Reed then kept the innings moving, Reed arriving with a sharper tempo and briefly giving the middle overs a second pulse before Ethan was finally removed by Dylan Hart. Reed also had to leave hurt after a brisk 39, and at that point Stonebridge might have hoped that two forced departures and a real wicket would cool the innings. Mason Hale made sure that did not happen. His unbeaten 45 was not just late decoration; it was the hand that kept Brookhaven’s final overs from flattening after the two retired batters had gone. Ryan Stone, Caleb Frost, Owen Pike, Finn Carter and Leo Ward all came through in shorter bursts, some useful, some messy, but Hale stayed as the constant, collecting from the gaps, taking on the fuller length when it appeared, and making sure every little lower-order fragment pushed the score further beyond normal reach. Stonebridge did keep taking wickets late, Marcus Flynn and Dylan Hart sharing the most visible reward, Caleb Price getting one, Henry Cole taking the opening break, and a run-out briefly giving the fielders something to shout about, but they never had the one sustained squeeze that could turn Brookhaven’s innings into a controlled score. The wides and the small extras hurt them as well, because against a side already carrying a hundred-plus retired hand, a half-century from Ethan Brooks, a second retired burst from Lucas Reed, and Hale still there at the close, every donation became expensive. Brookhaven finished on 338 for 7, and it felt like a total built in layers: Clarke’s start, Vale’s command, Brooks’ support, Reed’s heat, Hale’s finish, and enough lower-order motion to keep the final overs alive. Stonebridge’s chase needed something extraordinary, and what they produced was only a handful of usable fragments. Henry Cole and Marcus Flynn tried to make the first pocket respectable, but the required rate was already pressing on them before the innings had properly breathed, and when Owen Pike removed Henry, the reply lost one of the few batters who had looked settled enough to make time useful. Finn Carter then cut away Marcus, Daniel Shaw bowled Tyler Brooks, and although Logan Reed gave the chase its one real batting shape, it never truly became a pursuit. Logan’s 28 had some quality, especially through the stretch with Owen Mercer, and for a little while Stonebridge at least made Brookhaven keep working. The problem was that a chase this tall cannot survive on one small centre of resistance. Mason Hale broke the key passage by bowling Logan, then later removed Owen Mercer as well, and those wickets mattered because they did not simply add to a column, they stripped Stonebridge of the only pair that had started to make the innings look organized. Caleb Price was pinned by Caleb Frost, Dylan Hart tried to keep the score moving but fell to Owen Pike, and after that the lower order became a series of brief negotiations with the inevitable. Aaron Wells stayed for a while without finding a way to score quickly, Jacob Lane remained not out at the end, Oliver Grant came and went instantly, and Ben Carter’s last small push only delayed the finish. Ryan Stone’s late wickets gave Brookhaven the closing bite, while Mason Hale’s 3 for 20 was the most important bowling line because it removed the chase’s central batter and then broke the remaining structure. Stonebridge were all out for 111 in 29.3 overs, and the 227-run margin matched the actual balance of the day. This was not a match where one early burst alone decided everything; it was a match where Brookhaven kept winning successive phases until Stonebridge ran out of any credible route back. Vale gave the innings its size, Brooks and Reed made sure the middle did not stall, Hale gave it the finish and then helped control the defence, and the fielders stayed sharp enough to make the chase feel smaller with every passing over. Stonebridge had moments, especially through Logan Reed and a couple of late wickets in the first innings, but they never had a phase long enough to compete with Brookhaven’s best passages. Adrian Vale was the right player of the match because his 118 retired hurt was the innings around which everything else formed, and once that foundation was in place, Brookhaven turned a strong start into a crushing win.
